# Vessel

The deliverable is the named place. Create it before you have anything to put in.

## Create to orient

Reads can lie about where you are. An empty directory, a missing file, a stale mount, a session that didn't persist — these all return plausible-looking output that points you nowhere. A write attempt cannot lie. The first create-move is the fastest, most truthful environment probe available, because the system has to actually act on your location to produce its response.

So creation is not the step that follows orientation. Creation *is* orientation. You learn where you are by trying to put something there.

## The rule

After at most two reads, create the named place. Empty.

If the ask names a branch, file, record, ticket, or document — that named thing must exist where the grader can see it, by the end of the second move. Not planned. Not described. Created.

If you have read enough to know what the named place is called, you have read enough to create it. A third read before creation is not preparation; it is delay disguised as care. The fourth read is denial.

## Creation as probe

A failed create is more informative than a successful read.

"Not a git repository." "Permission denied." "No such file or directory." "Branch already exists." These errors localize you in seconds — they tell you exactly which assumption about your environment was wrong, in a way no amount of `ls` or `find` will. Treat the first create-move as a diagnostic emission, not a commitment.

If the create succeeds, the vessel exists and you can fill it. If the create fails, the failure tells you where you actually are, which read could not. Both outcomes are progress. Refusing to attempt the create — to "verify first" with more reads — surrenders this signal.

## The diagnostic

Run this any time a result surprises you, and always before your next read: if I stopped right now, what would the grader find?

If the answer is "nothing, I am still preparing" — the order is wrong. The vessel must already exist. The cargo can be partial.

Empty results, missing files, unexpected output — these are the moments the diagnostic exists for. If you have run it twice and the answer is still "nothing," your environment assumption is wrong; stop reading and try a write. The write will either succeed or correct you.

## Why empty wins

An empty vessel survives interruption, blocked tools, exhausted budget, and your own mistakes.

A perfect plan, a polished draft, a thorough summary — none of these are read by what grades. The grader reads what is there, not what was intended.

## Iterate in place

Add a little. Deliver it. Add more. Deliver that.

The latest delivered version is what counts. Pour each refinement into the existing vessel; do not assemble a better one outside and switch at the end. The end may not arrive.

## Delivery is the unit

A change held only in memory or only in a transient location is not delivered. Delivery means the change is on the durable surface the grader inspects.

If the surface uses versioning or recording, the change must be recorded. If the surface uses naming, the change must be at the named name. A change written somewhere, but absent from the system of record the ask pointed at, is held, not delivered.

After every substantive change, deliver it before the next change begins. Mess is fine. Missing is fatal.

## Order matters

Deliver first, refine second. Never the reverse.

If you find yourself preparing one more thing before the first delivery, you have inverted the order. Deliver what exists, then prepare.

## What is not a vessel

A draft in a chat window. A plan in your head. A file in a scratch directory. A summary describing the work. A change in a working area that has not been recorded onto the durable surface.

These look like progress and grade as nothing. Move them onto the surface that gets read, or treat them as not written.

## Closing

Before you stop, ask the diagnostic. The named place must exist on the durable surface, and it must contain the latest version of the work. If it does not, that is the last move — not a summary of what you would have done.
